Hello

HED: When birth control meets the algorithm

DEK: Desperate for information, young women are increasingly turning to TikTok for advice on contraceptives they can trust. Often, they find misinformation and ads instead.

By Jessica Blough

Tita Loyek understands better than most people how trends and views drive content. In 2020, the 29-year-old fashion influencer and her now husband packed up their New York City apartment and traveled across the country as digital nomads, documenting their journey on TikTok and picking up social media followers along the way.

At the same time while she was creating videos to feed the TikTok algorithm, she found herself ensnared in the very system she trusted. A family planning videostarted to pop up on her feed, prompted by her desire to start a family.  The videos she saw from other creators made her suspect that her years on birth control could have disrupted her hormones and impacted her fertility, and that she’d want to rebalance those hormones before she conceived.

She had the Nexplanon implant in her arm — a low-dose hormonal birth control option — removed, and instead started tracking her fertility using an Oura ring and an app called Natural Cycles.[a]

Natural Cycles is anFDA-approved birth control method that requires no hormones and isfavored by the Make America Healthy Again movement. Users input data on their basal body temperature, and the app uses an algorithm to give them a calendar of days when they can have sex with a very low risk of pregnancy, and when they should use additional protection. Natural Cycles is based on a method of birth control called fertility awareness, which is calendar-based and hormone-free.

With perfect use, doctors say that this type of birth control is 95 percent effective for the first year, and Natural Cycles says its algorithm model can swing that up to 99 percent. But with typical use, which accounts for human error, Natural Cycles’ effectiveness drops to a lower 93 percent. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists listed the effectiveness of fertility awareness methods in general as 77 percent with typical use.[b][c]

Within just a few months of use, Loyek received a notification from the app that one of her fertile days had been erroneously labeled as safe for unprotected sex. Shortly after, she took a pregnancy test, which came back positive.

According to Lauren Hanafin, a representative from Natural Cycles, just one in 200 women who use Natural Cycles in a year will become pregnant due to an error from the app, like Loyek. When Loyek reported her pregnancy to the company, it offered her a list of resources, including information on how to terminate it.

Though Loyek and her husband came to embrace the pregnancy, she was shocked and angry. “I just felt completely blindsided about it,” she said. “I didn't even know that was like a possibility that they could renege on those days and just be so wrong.”

In the five years since TikTok reached mass popularity in the United States, the platform has been used by young women to share medical advice with each other and, often, to offer alternatives to mainstream medical care through techniques like hormone balancing and holistic healthcare.

Content creators emphasize that their desire to create, spread, and seek out information about women’s health on social media comes from a place of feeling disenfranchised by doctors and the American healthcare system. Many of these women dealt with painful or irregular periods before they first came across videos describing symptoms or issues that sounded similar to theirs.

But researchers say these trends, which are largely dictated by TikTok’s algorithm and the app’s desire to increase views and engagement, skew towards demonizing hormonal birth control and undermining trust in doctors. They can impact how women like Loyek approach their health decisions.

A KFF study found that four in ten women have seen information about birth control on social media, and four in ten have shared it with another person. Fourteen percent of women ages 18 to 25 say that something they saw on social media made them change or consider changing their contraceptive methods.

In some of these videos, women blame hormonal birth control for vitamin deficiencies, depression and mood instability, low libido, and physical pain. In one popular genre of videos, young women unfurl the side-effect pamphlet from their birth control pills and use it as a blanket. Others edit together clips of them sobbing, with captions like “me on birth control.”

Some go further. In one video, a creator with the handle @back_inbalance claimed that birth control depleted vitamins, causing depression in young women. In another, @stirling_cooper spoke directly into a camera over ominous music, claiming that birth control was poisoning the minds and bodies of women. “Birth control is one of the most damaging things you can put in your body,” said a creator with the handle @theworkoutwitch.[d][e][f]

Does anyone else feel this way?

Frida Osuna, a student at University of Nevada, Los Angeles, has built a personal brand around "complaining and clothes.” In nearly all of her TikTok videos, she keeps her face close to her phone screen, nearly making eye contact with the viewer. To her 81,000 followers, she’s known for her hot, direct takes on politics, relationships, pet peeves, and not wanting to have children. Behind the screen, she said, she can “let it all out” and connect with people online who are looking for support in their unpopular opinions.

The majority of Osuna’s content is about her desire to not have children, and that includes sharing her positive experience with hormonal birth control and how it’s allowed her to prevent pregnancy.

“I can be someone’s, ‘My friend talked about this, and they said that it was okay,’” she said.

A2013 medical study popular among OBGYNs found that women are often influenced by the opinions of their friends and family when deciding what kind of birth control to go on. Interviews with multiple OBGYNs revealed that more and more patients have been asking them about what they heard from a stranger on TikTok.

Sharing health information, which often comes in the form of first-person accounts, has been in the social media landscape since before TikTok became popular, researcher Emily Pfender hypothesizes. Pfender started studying social media trends in women’s health in 2019, one of the first researchers to do so. Over the years, she’s looked at videos on cycle syncing and “what I eat in a day” videos as well as those about contraceptives.

On social media, personal reports are rarely checked for their veracity or created by medical professionals. And researchers like Pfender say that even social media accounts framed as personal experiences rather than medical advice can lead to changes. Social media videos tend to emphasize the risks of contraceptives that involve hormones, Pfender said, while decreasing the risks of other, nonhormonal methods.[g][h]

“This content has the potential to dissuade women from using hormonal contraceptives, which have a lot of value for pregnancy prevention, as well as health issues and medical issues,” Pfender said.

Hanafin from Natural Cycles said that the company creates the majority of its marketing materials based on personal accounts from women. That can include users who have had a negative experience with hormonal birth control.

Pfender herself is a content creator. For a researcher, she publishes frequently, but she wants her work to reach beyond academia and journal articles.

“The public doesn't care about reading journal articles,” she said. Her most popular videos tend to be those where she directly addresses hormones and birth control, like askit-style video on her Instagram page where she responds to a claim that hormonal birth control is responsible for the mental health crisis in the United States.

Narratives like these, which doctors say are false or misleading, get traction on social media. One claims that birth control can decrease fertility and make women sterile, which OBGYNs say is false. Claims that hormonal birth control can make women more attracted to other women than men, which were spread by Elon Musk on theTucker Carlson Network, are also false. Doctors also say that while prolonged use of birth control can increase risk of breast cancer, it also dramatically reduces the risk of ovarian cancer.

On YouTube, doctors can get verified as medical professionals and report misinformation to the platform, which will then take it down. TikTok doesn’t have those same protections or prioritize doctors in the same way. Due to Tiktok’s notorious content regulations, videos that refer to sex are often censored by the platform and removed.

Still, on TikTok, Dr. Jennifer Lincoln has built an audience of 2.8 million followers who come to her with questions about birth control, hormones, labor, and abortion. Speaking directly to the camera in nearly all her videos, the Portland-based OBGYN is often visibly pissed off by the quantity of misinformation that she encounters online, then tries to counteract.

Lincoln started making social media videos as a doctor in 2018, before TikTok existed. The platform is one of the worst for spreading true medical information, she said. And she worries about the consequences for those who fail to recognize bad information.

“I worry so much about the person who is watching this video who now isn’t going to seek care or try something that could literally save them from getting cancer of the uterus or being suicidal during their period,” Lincoln said. “I hate the idea that there are influencers out there who have no skin in the game, who will never be held accountable for the harm that they’re causing to some of these people.”[i]

VIDEO EMBED: https://www.tiktok.com/@drjenniferlincoln/video/7598579041867779358?lang=en

QUOTE: “I don’t love their marketing tone about hormones.”

— Dr. Jennifer Lincoln on Natural Cycles

“There's a whole new need for providers to engage with patients on their concerns and to listen to the concerns and to try to give them information in ways that they can absorb,” Cynthia Harper, director of Beyond the Pill at UCSF, said. Beyond the Pill is a research and resource program designed to provide comprehensive information on contraceptives to all people who need it, “early, often, and more than once,” Harper said. The organization has received over 100,000 requests for information from clinicians and patients across the country.

“Women want answers. A lot of women don't have answers, and a lot of women deal with not being believed. They deal with a lot of medical gaslighting and women's pain not taken seriously,” Pfender said. One of the early trends related to contraceptives on TikTok involved women filming themselves during IUD insertions, recording the painful cramping they experienced without any anesthetics. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, IUD insertion is “often painful or uncomfortable.” ACOG recommended further research into addressing this pain for the comfort of patients.

That fear of pain and distrust in medicine can be steered on TikTok to increase views and sell products or services through “scare tactics.”

“The videos where women were talking about being medically disenfranchised, they got significantly more engagement,” Pfender said.

The rise of the “natural” right

Branna Grace Reed wasn’t prepared to be a mother this early, but she has embraced it. From her home in rural Montana, Reed, 26, posts videos of her feeding chickens, baking cookies, and breastfeeding her daughter to her modest followers, blue skies and green mountains in the background. On TikTok, she’d documented her planning process and transition from the Tennessee mountains to Montana life. One on one, she’s forthcoming and warm, her voice retaining its deep southern accent.

On a video call, her six month old daughter coos quietly next to her, then more insistently until Reed picks her up. Reed pauses periodically to turn her attention toward the baby, still in pink pajamas well into the afternoon, and protectively tries to keep her daughter’s face away from the screen. She wears a gold wedding ring and matching Oura ring on the fingers of her left hand.[j]

The Oura ring is part of the reason she got pregnant with her daughter, earlier than expected. After she got married, Reed had been tracking her cycle with Natural Cycles and admits, embarrassed, that she read the app’s recommendations wrong, leading to her pregnancy.

Fertility awareness is one of the most complicated forms of birth control to use, Harper said. Especially for patients who might struggle with the regularity of taking a daily pill, fertility awareness has much higher demands.

Reed was put on the birth control pill when she was a teenager and said she felt like she had little choice in the matter. She later stopped hormonal birth control with the supervision of a doctor, but she’s gone through periods of skepticism about artificial dyes, antibiotics, chemicals, and toxins that have caused her extreme anxiety. After intervention from her family, she’s trying to seek more balance and hold more doubt for what she sees online.

“You can get so much on there, but I had to be mindful of what was fear mongering versus trying to educate people,” Reed said. “If I feel like I'm getting scared from content that I'm consuming or information that is being thrown at me, I have to take a step back.”

Simultaneously, the far right of the United States and the Make America Healthy Again movement are actively encouraging people to get off hormonal contraceptives and pushing methods that are dubbed more “natural” and nonhormonal, like fertility awareness. In a TikTok video with 4.2 million views, Musk claims on the Tucker Carlson Network that hormonal birth control causes depression, increases risk of suicide, and makes women choose partners that they wouldn’t select if they were not on the pill.

Federal cuts to Medicaid and Title X are likely to make it more difficult for people to access contraceptives and pay for them, and millions of Americans lost abortion access after the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization decision in 2022, which overturned Roe v. Wade.

VIDEO EMBED: https://www.tiktok.com/@tuckercarlsonnetwork/video/7423799850791144747

QUOTE: “A lot of women are unaware that hormonal birth control causes depression and dramatically increases risk of suicide and changes their preferences on who they want to marry or have kids with. It changes their personality.”

— Elon Musk on the Tucker Carlson Show. Doctors say that this is categorically false.

Communications researchers are careful to separate their work from any political motivations or calculations. But the need for reliable information in an ecosystem that lacks a consistent check on misinformation comes up at the edges of their work. Pfender will take to social media herself, her credentials in her bio. “I didn’t become a scientist to go viral—but silence on social media hurts women’s health,” reads one of her pinned posts.

That need is accentuated, she said, by how much content on social media about contraceptives and women’s health is tied to advertising a product. Product marketing is built into TikTok’s business model, and Pfender has noticed the prevalence of fear-based language in these advertisements. For example, in videos that warn women that their hormones might be disrupted by birth control use and vulnerability to infertility, content creators often direct women back to fitness and health packages or subscriptions, or an Amazon storefront full of supplements. “They use that and repurpose it to basically sell women products and services that they don't really need, that are not evidence based,” Pfender said.

“People will throw words around, like hormone balancing or endocrine disruptors or infertility,” Reed said. “If someone's throwing constant products at you, I'm like, well, you're just trying to make money off these people trying to figure out their health, especially women.”

Natural Cycles, the app that Reed and Loyek were using when they got pregnant and physicians are wary of because of its complicated definition of perfect use, runs advertisements on social media and pays influencers to create sponsored posts. It also charges a monthly subscription fee for its users, starting at $16.99 and including a basal thermometer. Users can also pair the app with their Apple Watch or Oura Ring for temperature measurements and sleep tracking.

Hanafin from Natural Cycles denied that the company has purposely profited off the country’s rightward shift. “Those are conversations that we want no part of,” she said.

But the selling point for young women can be the personalization of stories about birth control on social media. Erin Ash, a professor in health communications at Clemson University, began studying birth control on social media after a conversation with her daughter, a preteen at the time, who said she refused to get on hormonal birth control because it could make her depressed or gain weight, rumors she’d seen on social media. Beginning in 2023, Ash reviewed 1600 videos of women talking about contraceptives on social media, each with over 100,000 views. Like Loyek’s video, the majority were based on personal anecdotes that communicated a specific experience.

“Narratives are extremely effective,” Ash notes.

Ash works on a team of three at Clemson with CJ Calabrese and Ashley McKenzie, all communications professors who study health and media. While Ash led the video analysis portion of the project, McKenzie conducted a series of interviews with influencers on why they post information related to contraceptives on social media.

The results, she said, surprised her: the dominant motivation that influencers reported for sharing their stories about contraceptives on social media wasn’t profit or engagement. Instead, the 15 women she talked to expressed a sense of genuine care for their audience and a desire to help other women, even when the information they were sharing was not factually accurate or missing critical nuance.

But when this desire to share information comes in the form of medical skepticism, it can have real, physical effects.

Researchers at Sheffield University led by Rebecca Webster found that young women who have doubts about the pill, have been exposed to counter narratives about modern medicine, or are distrustful of the healthcare system report worse side effects from being on hormonal birth control. They dubbed this psychological phenomenon the “nocebo” effect, the opposite of the placebo effect.

“They're still very real side effects that people are experiencing that women are experiencing,” Webster said. “If we have more information, we can try and deal with this and combat it to make people's experience with the pill better and more positive, so they don't feel that they have to just stop taking it or switch to something that's less effective.”

The consequences can be dangerous. Webster gave an example of the rollout of the HPV vaccine rollout in 2013 in Japan: shortly after it became available, unfounded reports of side effects of the vaccine on girls circulated through social media, gaining traction until Japan halted the vaccination program. The Japanese government didn’t recommend the vaccine, which can help prevent cervical cancer, until 2021.

A growing countermovement

Today, Loyek is still posting on TikTok, sharing glimpses of days in her life with her 190,000 followers. Instead of hunting for sample sales, she’s looking for apartments big enough to host her growing family. After a miscarriage, which she documented on TikTok, she’s pregnant again, due at the beginning of May. After her daughter is born, she said she’ll get back on birth control, likely going back to a hormonal method.

“Definitely not Natural Cycles,” she said.

Reed, on the other hand, has cut back significantly on her posting. She hides her daughter’s face and name from social media, focusing instead on her role as a mother. She received some hate messages on TikTok when she shared her experience with Natural Cycles, and the response has made her withdrawn and skeptical.

“It did change my perspective and how I consume when I watch and judge other people's content,” she said. “I would never go out of my way, especially not to another woman, to comment on what she decided for her health.”

While reporting this story, my personal experience began to creep in. I started looking into this topic after my doctor took me off a high dose hormonal birth control in 2023, warning that a combination of health symptoms led me to have a high stroke risk. It was a scary and shocking conversation, and I was surprised to later see from content creators on TikTok discussing the same set of symptoms and physician reaction that I’d experienced. When painful migraine headaches debilitated me and kept me from work, school, and relationships, I wanted to blame something and turned first to my new birth control. I was wrong.[k]

But for many young women, the sense of who to trust is slipping. Doctors office appointments are harder to get, and the costs of medical care and insurance are rising. The CDC eliminated the segment of its reproductive health unit that handles best practices around contraceptives. Large segments of the country have no gynecologists. TikTok is free, and it’s easy to access, and it’s already where so many young people are.[l][m]

McKenzie and Ash, the researchers at Clemson University, are already thinking about their next research project, a toolkit to help content creators spot misinformation on social media and spread more health-informed information. Pfender makes TikTok videos debunking common myths she’s seeing on social media and sharing her research. Beyond the Pill, the UCSF project run by Harper, trains clinicians to empower patients in their contraceptive choices and educate them on what they’re able to access.

Doctors, too, are taking to social media. In videos quickly recorded on her lunch break or on a walk, Dr. Caledonia Buckheit answers questions from her followers about how IUDs work and what to expect from perimenopause. Buckheit has a fraction of the follower count that Lincoln does, and her most popular videos only get a few thousand views. Still, she wishes more of her fellow healthcare providers were willing to get on screen and talk directly to larger audiences of patients, who fill her comments with more questions.

Some patients who walk into her office confess that they’ve traveled for hours after seeing her TikTok videos. They pick her as their doctor because they believe she’ll listen to them when they say they want their tubes tied or to find a new treatment for PCOS.

“Patients have negative experiences. I know how this happens,” Buckheit said. “They drive hours to come and see me, and they’re like, ‘It’s because I saw you on social media and I knew that you would take me seriously.’”

VIDEO EMBED: https://www.tiktok.com/@sandyboston/video/7429493034095512862

QUOTE: “There’s a lot of all natural things that I do in my life, and I don’t feel like birth control is something that’s gonna ruin my health.”

— Cassandra Gallagher went viral for a video about how much she loves her birth control.

And some content creators, like Osuna, are recognizing the need for different stories on social media about birth control. Some defend their birth control in impassioned videos, warning their followers to be skeptical of ads and scare tactics on social media. Those videos express gratitude, and even love, for hormonal birth control.

The question is if these counter-narratives by doctors, researchers, and creators will be effective enough to reach the young women who are searching for answers, or if the algorithm is already too far ahead of them to catch.
